subtopic: TRANSFEB TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY

speechtext:
The house resumed from Thursday, March 17, consideration in committee of Bill No. 21, to amend the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act-Mr. Mackenzie King-Sir Eugene Fiset in the chair.
Section 3 agreed to.
On section 4-On export of power.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: TRANSFEB TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
TRANSFEB TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext:
All licences for the export of power granted prior to the passing of this bill will expire each year on March 31, whereas power which might be disposed of under a

private act would be for a term fixed by the private act. I should think that in all conscience this bill should provide that every private bill shall be subject to the control which we now exercise, namely, that the licence shall expire on the thirty-first day of March. The private bill should be based upon the same principle as that which has governed us heretofore in granting such permission to export power. The other evening the Prime Minister brought forward the Canadian Power Company case as indicating a licence to export power. I confess that at that moment I was not aware of the fact that this was the present Ontario Power Company, but that private act did not contain in any part of it a provision for the export of power. It merely provided that they could carry the wires across the bridge and connect them up; in no place in that act did it say that any power was to be exported. So far as I have been able to find out, nowhere in the Canadian statutes is there any private act that authorizes the export of power.
In support of that position all you have to do is look at the white book, where you will see that this very company has had to take out its annual licence, and the footnote indicates that the rights of the old Canadian Power Company under chapter 120 of the statutes of 1887 were acquired by the Ontario Power Company, the rights of that company in turn being acquired by the hydro-electric commission. As I say, the provisions of that statute did not contain a single reference to the export of power, but they did contemplate the connecting up of the Canadian company with the American company, and it provided that they might make an arrangement to work the said electric light or other power jointly. But they were very careful not to say anything about the export of power.
Should we not maintain a measure of uniformity in connection with this matter? Here are the licences for the export of power, at pages 97 and 98 of the white book. Those licences, as I say, are allowed to run for only a year and expire, I repeat, on March 31, as I understand it. But they are renewable in the terms of the licences, in the absence of any understanding or event that might make it undesirable so to do. I put this point to the Minister of Justice. Yesterday the United States declared that they do not desire to import power from Canada. That relieves this situation very greatly. So far as this bill is concerned it can have no bearing in relation to the United States, and I do not know of any other country to which we would export power. Under the circum-

Electric Power Export
stances is it desirable to have one statute under which licences expire on the 31st day of March in each year and, assuming that conditions changed, another set of exports or sales in connection with which the term is fixed by private acts? I think not. I strenuously object to the export of a part of Canada being provided for in a private act brought in by a private member. The very theory itself is contrary to our system of government; that is, that a private member should introduce a private act by petition under which a part of this dominion may be exported out of this country, fixing in the terms of his bill-not the general act-the provision as to how long this is to be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: TRANSFEB TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext: It is parliament that does that.

subtopic: TRANSFEB TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext:
Of course parliament
passes every private act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: TRANSFEB TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext: It is not a private member who will decide on that.

subtopic: TRANSFEB TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext:
But the private member introduces the measure and indicates to the house his idea as to what should be done; and that bill, as it is presented to the house, necessarily will contain a statement as to the period of time during which that power can be exported. If it is important that we should have these other provisions in what you might call a regulated plan, then is it not more important still that we should have a period of time fixed within which these exports can be carried on, especially having regard to the observations made by the utilities board of New York, and the order in council passed in 1914 against the acquisition of vested rights in connection with any such exports? It may be purely academic now in view of the dispatch from the United States, but obviously should not the standard be set in the enabling statute and not in the private act?
I mention that because, I repeat, in the act as it will leave this house we shall have provided that the sales now authorized shall be renewed only from year to year, unless, in view of the dispatch from the United States indicating that they do not desire to import power from Canada, these licences will not be renewed. In any case it is distinctly provided that there is no acquisition of a right by reason of the licences now in existence. I say this in no contentious or controversial sense, but I do think that in order to prevent the possibility of a vested right being acquired under any private act fixing a period of time during which power may be exported, it would be desirable in the enabling statute, if I might call this such, not only to provide what we
have provided with respect to surplus power, the price at which it can ibe sold, and the punishment or penalty or sanction, if I may use the word, for disregard of the terms of the private act-loss of the right to export; we should do also what we do in the Bank Act or the Railway Act or the Trust Companies Act or any of the other acts which deal with the essential point of the period of time, and indicate in the standard enabling act, which this will now become, the period during which the export could take place. For, as I say, on the one hand we will have a licence and on the other a private act, both authorizing the export of power. One will be for the term fixed by the private act and the other will be for the term fixed by the enabling statute, which makes it clear beyond peradventure that no vested rights are being acquired and that on the 31st day of March in each year there must be a termination of the right to export; and that a new right arises only as it is confirmed by the renewal of the licence, or, in the case of a private act, as might be thought desirable by reason of there being no controversy as to surplus power or price or as to the performance by the selling company of all the obligations placed upon it by the statute.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: TRANSFEB TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext: Of course the suggestions made by my right hon. friend relate rather to a question of policy. I may say that the three alternatives have been considered in the preparation of the bill, namely the one which is now before the house, leaving it to parliament to fix the number of years during which this permission to export will be granted, but with subsection (c) of section 4, which allows the governor in council to repeal it at any time.

subtopic: TRANSFEB TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext: Upon giving notice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: TRANSFEB TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext: Upon giving notice, because of course private interests may be affected, and it is only fair that notice should be given.

subtopic: TRANSFEB TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext: There is no objection to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: TRANSFEB TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext:
But if a repeal is being made because of the failure of the grantees to act according to the provisions of the bill, then it will be without notice- namely, if it exports power which is not surplus power, or if it charges a lower price in a foreign country than is charged to a Canadian consumer.
Perhaps I should read subsection (c) again:
The said private act may be repealed by proclamation of the governor in council at any time upon such notice as the governor in
Electric Power Export

council shall prescribe, or, if the governor in council is satisfied that the conditions imposed by paragraph (a) or (b) -
That is, the surplus of power and the price to be charged-
-of this subsection are not being complied with, without notice.
As it is, we leave to parliament the discretion as to the number of years during which the bill will be in force.
Then we considered another alternative, which would have been adding another paragraph, namely paragraph (d), in these words:
Subject to the provisions of paragraph (c) in this subsection-
The one I have just read-
-the said private act shall remain in force for a period of five years from the date of the commencement thereof.
This would have fixed the time limit. After five years the law would have disappeared altogether. Then we considered another alternative, the one which my right hon. friend opposite seems to favour-if I may have his attention.

subtopic: TRANSFEB TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext: I am listening carefully.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: TRANSFEB TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext:
It would be paragraph (d) and in these words:
Subject to the provisions of paragraph (c) of this subsection the said private act shall remain in force for a period of one year from the date of the commencement thereof, but may be extended from year to year by proclamation of the governor in council for four yearly periods of one year each, but not so that the said act shall in any case remain in force for more than five years from the date of the commencement thereof.
There again it would be limited to five years, renewable by proclamation every year.
But as I have said, this is rather a question of policy. I must say-and I think I am right in saying this-that the government is not linked with any one of those methods, and if the committee favours the suggestion of my right hon. friend opposite I think we would be quite willing to require the new proclamation every year to keep the act in force for a certain number of years.

subtopic: TRANSFEB TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext:
The white book indicates that in 1907 licences were issued to the Canadian Niagara Power Company of Niagara Falls, Ontario. It is stated that the transmission line crosses the boundary at or near Fort Erie and Niagara Falls, Ontario, the licence for firm power starting in 1908 with 39,165 kilowatts and rising to 45,000 kilowatts in 1938. Then there is a note which says:

These companies were under the control of the electric power controller for these years, and licences were not issued by this department. The amounts shown are those recommended by the power controller.
Then for the same company, and with the same statement as to transmission line, dealing with surplus returnable on demand, the licence was issued in 1925, eighteen years later, and began to operate in 1926 with 20,000 kilowatts.
Then we turn to page 98, and we find mention of the Ontario Power Company of Niagara Falls, Ontario. It is stated that the transmission line crossed the boundary at or near Niagara Falls, Ontario. The date of the original licence was November 9, 1907. That was for firm power, beginning with 45,000 kilowatts, and is still for that amount, although at one time it rose to 60,000 kilowatts, and then fell to 37,300 kilowatts in two years. Note (a) is as follows:
This company was under the control of the electric power controller for these years and licence was not issued by this department.
That was during the period of the war, in the years 1918 and 1919. Then, note (b) states:
The Electrical Development Company and The Ontario Power Company were purchased by the Hydro-Electric Power Commission, and a licence equal to the sum of the licences of these two companies was obtained by the Hydro-Electric Power Commission.
That is one for 80,000 kilowatts, the first licence having been issued in 1925. It has now, in 1938, fallen to 45,000 kilowatts, and the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario, at another spot near Queenston, has the right this year to export 80,000 kilowatts.
These are the two relevant licences in the province of Ontario. Of course, there is a licence in New Brunswick for 2,500 kilowatts; there is another one for 2,500 kilowatts, and there is one in Ontario, at Fort Frances, for 5,500 kilowatts. The point I should like to make is that under the terms of licences the hydro commission now has, it can export its power only for one year, the licence expiring on the 31st day of March in each year. There is no right of renewal, qua right, but it is renewed if the power is not required, and the company has conformed to all the requirements of the department.
Now comes the next point: If you grant a licence for five years, not stating how to divide it up, you have created a vested right, unless you add another paragraph, such as I suggested the other day, that no renewal of licence or any other act shall create a vested interest under this act. That, I believe, is important in view of what was said-and even

Electric Power Export
in the dispatch which we had yesterday, there was the same thing. What are the grounds upon which the Secretary of State of the United States has placed his refusal? He says: "We do not desire to import power into the United States". First of all he refers to the protection of his power market. That is number one. Then, as number two, he refers to the undesirability of importing power from a foreign country, and thirdly, he casually mentioned the question of defence. On those three grounds the matter is put, and the opinion of Attorney General McReynolds is used as a basis, since the repeal of the Burton Act.
Now we are going to have the same hydroelectric commission apply for a private act in this parliament?-for they are the only applicants at the present time for the export of power. That private act may contain a provision for a term of years. But the licences they will have at Queenston and Niagara Falls will expire on the 31st day of March in each year, so that no vested right can arise, we have made it so clear as to be beyond the possibility of doubt. If, however, we pursue the course suggested in connection with a private act, what we have done-whatever language we may use, if we use a term of years at all, unless we negative it by express language-is to create a vested right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: TRANSFEB TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext: In favour of whom?

subtopic: TRANSFEB TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext: In favour of the hydroelectric commission.

subtopic: TRANSFEB TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext:
We reserve the right to
cancel at the end of another year.

subtopic: TRANSFEB TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext:
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) grasps at once the point I am desiring to make, that is, that the licence has to be uniform. The private act, which is a licence, should conform, so far as uniformity is concerned, to the licence which is being maintained by this statute. Remember, this statute maintains the licence feature. There must be no misunderstanding about that. The language of the section was redrawn the other evening to make it clearer. At Queenston there is the question of 80,000 kilowatts and at Niagara Falls, 45,000 kilowatts; in both cases the licences expire on March 31 of each year. But you have another licence in the form of a private act, so called, which authorizes the export, we will say for the sake of argument, of 50,000 kilowatts over a period of years. That is a creation of a vested right. In order that there may be uniformity we should see that the right to export power under this private act shall expire on March
31 in each year, but may be renewed, by the governor in council if you like, from year to year, just as the main act now says with respect to Queenston and Niagara Falls power.
We would thus have uniformity at Fort Frances, in Maine, at Niagara Falls and at Kingston. All would be in the same position. We now have the anomaly of having a private act authorizing for a period the export of power from this country without having the safeguards that are established by the general statute. I am not saying this in any captious sense, because so far as I am concerned the matter is of complete indifference. I am putting it forward in the public interest. There should be uniformity, and the Minister of Justice has indicated that two or three alternatives were considered. All I suggest is that you combine the three of them. First, you would provide for no period at all. The private act should make it clear that no period is being contemplated, the same as is now the case with Niagara Falls power. Remember we are dealing with exactly the same people. The only applicants we have before us are those who have the licence for the power at Queenston and Niagara Falls. Let us give them their licences in the same terms. They have not complained; they have been satisfied,
Then there are the two provisions that have been added, namely, one with respect to surplus power and price, which I think is admirable, and one with respect to the right to repeal the statute by proclamation. That is such a vast extension of the power of the governor in council that I could hardly see my learned and right hon. friend, the Minister of Justice, make the statement without choking, having regard to his attitude in times past with respect to the abuse of power by the governor in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: TRANSFEB TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext: We have it already.

subtopic: TRANSFEB TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext: It was against that that the Prime Minister the other day quoted the authqrity of Sir Robert Borden and others to the effect that it was a terrible thing to contemplate the possibility of the governor in council doing it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: TRANSFEB TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext: We have too much power now.

subtopic: TRANSFEB TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext:
We are suggesting that
it might be dealt with in this way. In any system of responsible government some power must be given to the executive to deal with certain phases of the matter. I think you could meet the situation with a combination of the three. First, provide that any
Electric Power Export

authority to export power under any private act shall expire on March 31 in each year. Second, such right may be renewed from year to year, just as we have it in the principal statute. Third, nothing in this contained shall confer any right. All these the minister has in his mind in the provisions he has added. There is not one suggestion not contained in the combination of his three. If you combine the three of them, everything is there. Possibly I am a little stronger on the question of the acquisition of a vested right and the exact language, but if you combine the three I submit you have everything. It is in the public interest to maintain uniformity in all grants to export, whether they be for the company at Queenston, which is the same company, or the one at Niagara Falls or here.
That is the point I desired to make. I do not know whether I have made it plain, but I wanted to clear up beyond any per-adventure the statement to which reference was made the other evening, that the Canadian Power Company statute does confer any right to export. On the contrary, it does not. What is more, they had to take out a licence and they have taken out a licence. The statute changing the name to the Ontario Power Company was chapter 105 of 1899, and that company was acquired by the hydro electric commission. The commission has taken out a licence from year to year. That is all I desire to say. Perhaps I could crystallize it into a really clear statement, but I think the point is quite apparent to the Minister of Justice.

subtopic: TRANSFEB TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext: The record shows clearly that notwithstanding the fact that licences have been issued annually, and that they contain restrictions and provisions for cancellation, after having been in force for years, there has grown up in the United States the contention, notwithstanding all this, that vested rights may be acquired. If we pass an act of parliament and say that power may be exported for five years instead of one, surely we will be giving that contention just five times the weight which it has under the existing statute. That is the serious matter in this whole proposition. We should guard in every way against the possibility of the contention arising that there is a vested right. This should be done to prevent any international difficulty. It does seem to me that uniformity should exist in connection with these licences, and the course outlined by my leader provides for this. It would not require much change in the drafting of the amendment to secure this result, and I think it is most desirable.

subtopic: TRANSFEB TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to discuss the provisions of this section very shortly before it is passed and call to the attention of the committee some matters which I think will -be helpful in determining in just what way we should leave section 4, when viewed in the light of the amendments and the original draft.
Hon. members will recall that the section provides, first, that in future power exportation can be had only by an applicant coming to parliament with a private bill instead of as heretofore; second, that there must accompany the application an order in council from the exporting province-in the case of the hydro commission it would be Ontario-and where the power is generated wholly or in part in another province, there shall be also an order in council from the generating province. It is the intention of this amendment, I think quite properly, to see to it that both such provinces shall first express their approval of authorization to any private person, corporation or public utility to export power. I desire to align myself with the idea put forward by the leader of the opposition, (Mr. Bennett) namely, that we should provide if possible that, once by private act parliament has authorized a new and further export of power, thereafter there should be power by annual licence to continue and renew the export which parliament has once approved. It would be folly to ask any proposed exporter to come back year by year to parliament for a private bill to continue exportation. The proposed amendment sees fit to preserve by order in council the right to renew all existing licences. That perhaps is an added reason why we should deal most carefully with legislation for the export of power.
Since the first application early in January by the hydro commission of Ontario, backed as it was by the premier of Ontario, for leave to export power, there has been a deliberate and organized effort by the Conservative party of Ontario and the Conservative federal party to kill the application. Yes-I beg the hon. member's pardon. However, the point I wish to make is that the bill before us is a general one which relates to applications for the right to export power which may be made at any time from any part of Canada. It is not a bill relating only to an application which may come from Ontario, respecting the hydroelectric commission. It is a bill which will pertain equally to applications which may come from Manitoba, British Columbia, New Brunswick or any other province, and which may be made at any time in the future.
What we are therefore immediately concerned with is the framing of a measure which will serve as a guide to those who may apply in the future for the right to export power, and to set out certain provisions a private bill should contain if its sponsors expect it to be approved by the parliament of Canada. The reason why the restrictive conditions were not included in the general bill is not that the government hoped to have more freedom in granting an applicant but, on the contrary, it was because the government desired to give to parliament the freedom to insert in a private bill any provision it might wish. It did seem to the administration a little inconsistent to say, on the one hand, " We will leave to parliament the whole question of granting an application, in the form of a private bill," and at the same time not leave parliament free to insert in the private bill any provision it might wish to insert.
It would be assumed, I believe, that a private bill would designate the number of years for which the right to export would be granted. That would be one of the first provisions which would be considered. In some cases it might be a bill to permit the export of power for one or two years. To name five years definitely as a period beyond which no private bill should continue in force might, on the face of it, appear to be an invitation to applicants to make applications for bills which in all cases would have a duration of five years. Similarly, the necessity of the government renewing a licence from year to year was a provision which, it was assumed by the administration, parliament itself would insert in a private bill, if it was thought that such provision were necessary and desirable.
That is the reason why these provisions, in detail, were not set forth in the bill, as originally presented. Where parliament gives

certain power to the governor in council and leaves the final word with that body, there is a special reason for restricting and limiting the governor in council with respect to time and with respect to other provisions of which account should be taken. If it will help to effect unanimity with respect to the present measure, I see no reason why the committee should not accept the provision mentioned by the right hon. Minister of Justice. It is one which the government has considered and which it was prepared to bring before the committee for its consideration if there appeared to be a desire to have it presented. I shall ask the minister later on to move the amendment he has proposed. We now have three subsections, (a), (b) and (c), and the following is proposed by the hon. Minister of Justice as a new subsection (d):
Subject to the provisions of paragraph (c) of this subsection, the said private act shall remain in force for a period of one year from the date of the commencement thereof, but may be extended from year to year by proclamation of the governor in council for four further periods of one year each, but not so that the said act shall in any case remain in force for more than five years from the date of the commencement thereof.

It seems to me that the proposed additional amendment solves the difficulty that existed before and should meet with the unanimous approval of the committee. Some gentlemen questioned whether the Ontario hydro application would have passed. That is in the realm of speculation and nobody can say. However, in order to afford a guide in the future, should there be a change of policy on the part of the executive of the United States-a thing quite possible and thinkable in these days when changes occur so fast-may I suggest that practically every province of Canada is to-day enjoying a revenue from the United States dollars which come into Canada to pay for the export of surplus power. I refuse to believe that hon. gentlemen from British Columbia, New Brunswick, Manitoba and Quebec, each of which provinces is enjoying revenue from the export of surplus power, will join in the cabal of the other side to prohibit Ontario from having the right to export power which the engineers state is undoubtedly surplus.
The executive of the United States has observed that we in Canada have great undeveloped natural power resources, while in the eastern states particularly the power resources are practically all exhausted, inasmuch as they have all been brought into development at the present time. Let us keep that in mind, in endeavouring to get an enactment of section 4 which looks towards the future in a broad

Electric Power Export
way. I should like to give in that respect some figures which I obtained from page 387 of the Canada Year Book for 1936. These figures indicate the available and developed water power in Canada by provinces, as of January, 1936. The two most important provinces in this respect are, first, Quebec, and next, Ontario, I shall not give the figures for the other provinces as those who are interested further may go to the Canada Year Book for them. The figures for Quebec show that the available 24-hour power at 80 per cent efficiency is 8,459,000 horse power at the ordinary minimum flow, and 13,064,000 at the ordinary six months' flow. The total turbine installation as of that date was 3,853,320 horse power. In the case of Ontario, the available power at 80 per cent efficiency, at ordinary minimum flow, was 5,330,000 horse power; at ordinary six months' flow, 6,940,000 horse power, while the turbine installation totalled 2,560,155 horse power.
We may look forward to an influx of United States, British and other capital to help to develop the undeveloped water power across Canada. Therefore we must be careful not to declare for future generations and not to put upon the records of parliament any false notions of economy as to the desirability, if at any time it be found desirable, of inviting capital to develop further these great natural resources. These times of stress, which have been noted before in the house, are peculiarly the time when we should fall in with the views of the president of the United States. I believe in him sufficiently to assume that if conditions change and if it is thought desirable to indicate to Canada a different policy, he will do so; for I am sure it is his desire, as it is and always has been the Liberal policy, to promote good will, the attitude of the good neighbour, and friendly and kindly relations between the two countries.

I commend the Prime Minister for bringing this discussion back to a consideration of the merits of the bill now before the committee. The hon. member for Parry Sound certainly has made one of the most provocative speeches I have ever heard in this chamber since I became a member. If I had not too much respect for myself, for the Prime Minister, for the leader of the opposition and for other hon. members, I would retaliate in phrases which would be quite as sharp and poignant as those which he has attempted to toss across the floor of the chamber this afternoon. It was not commendable for the hon. gentleman; it reflected no credit upon him that he should assume to fling across the chamber the epithets which he did this afternoon. If he persists in that 51052-XOOi
course he will not hereafter find his membership in this house as pleasant and agreeable as it has been during the present and the two previous sessions. So far as I am concerned, I have heard of no cabal on either side of the house against the Ontario government or the Ontario Hydro Electric Power Commission. If such a cabal exists, either on the government side or on this side, it certainly has not been mentioned in any of the private discussions which I have had with colleagues on both sides with regard to the merits of this bill.
When the Prime Minister introduced the bill I accepted it as an effort on the part of the government, after due and careful consideration, to amend the statute of 1907, the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act, and to provide that parliament might give an unbiased consideration to any future application for the export of power. The fact that the hon. member for Parry Sound intended to introduce some special measure in this case was not mentioned to me and was not known by me, and I did not take any observations on the possibility of a private bill being brought before the house to be a reflection upon the premier of Ontario, or upon the commission which my hon. friend represents, or to refer to the prospective introduction of a bill by the hon. member. I have tried to consider this matter not solely from the point of view of Ontario, because Ontario's interests are not so well known to me; I was also considering it from the point of view of other provinces, such as Quebec, which now have and will have in future large quantities of hydro-electric power for exportation, if the hydro-electric diversions which now exist and others which are in contemplation in those provinces are brought to completion.
In all his discussions with myself and my colleagues the leader of the opposition has always sought to ascertain what, in our opinion, would be fair and proper provisions to suggest by way of amendment to the bill now before the committee, not with a view to precluding hydro-electric development in Ontario, not with the view of placing obstacles in the way of the premier of Ontario and his government, or in the way of the hydroelectric commission of Ontario, but with a view to ascertaining and, if possible, enacting provisions which would apply to all possible applications for the export of power in the immediate future.
To suggest that this law which we now place on the statute books will be like the laws of the Medes and Persians, never to be amended or modified, is nonsense. That there

is any such intention in the mind of the Prime Minister, it would be, I think, nonsensical to assert. We are dealing to the best of our intelligence with conditions at present existing in order to frame a general law under which the export of power in future may be carried on with the full approval not only of this house but of both houses of parliament. In that purpose I concur. Therefore, when the bill came before the house and amendments were suggested, we on this side suggested certain amendments which, in conversation among ourselves, had occurred to us, and from a desire solely to assist in drafting a bill which would commend itself to the great majority of this house. In discussing this bill I think we might just as well leave Ontario, as Ontario, and the interests of the hydro-electric of Ontario, out of consideration.
The suggestions which were made as to possible caballing for private ends remain, because whenever private acts are applied for, which grant or propose to grant special rights or privileges to certain sections of the country or to certain groups of individuals, there is always a tendency to caballing and lobbying. Such remarks as were made on this side of the house apply, I am sure, to that prospective condition of affairs and had no application to the hon. member for Parry Sound or to the interests which he represents in this particular debate. Therefore I suggest to the committee that we should accept the declaration of the Prime Minister as to his intentions in introducing this bill and his reasons for proposing certain amendments to the bill, and then, without further consideration of the provocative statements made by the hon. member for Parry Sound, we should give our full attention and apply the best of our intelligence and experience to the modification of this bill so that it may meet with the full approval of the great majority of members on both sides. That is the only aim which I have in view.

I wish to say just a word or two in reply to the extraordinary speech to which we listened this afternoon. I do not mind any hon. member making a speech, and I realize that perhaps one of the hardest things any prospective speaker has to endure is to have a speech which has been kept, so to speak, in cold storage for many months. Some day he wants to deliver it, and probably this afternoon we have had an example of the speech that has to be delivered, this being the only opportunity to present it. But probably it would have been better had it never been delivered. It is not pleasant to have statements made in this chamber which have a sinister reference to other hon.

members, and such statements should not be made unless they can be backed up by absolute proof. When the hon. member for Parry Sound used the word "cabal," I thought I would send to the parliamentary library for the Encyclopedia Britannica and see what the word really meant. This is what I find:
Cabal:	A private organization * or party
engaged in secret intrigues and applied also to the intrigues themselves.
I have been in this chamber during the whole time that this measure has been before the house, and I know of no secret intrigues that have been carried on. Now and again I have spoken to hon. members with reference to this bill. I know some Liberal members who are very much opposed to the measure, and probably, if a private bill carrying out the intents and purposes of the legislation now under consideration came before us, they would vote against it. But as to any member who had it in his mind to vote against such a bill being accused of doing something that is against all rhyme and reason, I cannot understand language of that kind being used in connection with such a matter.
The hon. member wanted to know what Liberals were opposed to this measure. He does not need to go outside Ontario to discover that. In the provincial house there is the hon. member for Bellwoods, the former attorney general, who probably knows as much as any man in Ontario about hydro affairs. I do not think it can be said that Mr. Roebuck, M.L.A. for Bellwoods, is in favour of the proposals that were enunciated here this afternoon by the hon. member for Parry Sound. I believe we have all heard within the last few days the statements in which Mr. Arthur Roebuck has scathingly denounced the whole of these proposals, and there is in those proposals a good deal which deserves, probably, close consideration by hon. members. If members are not prepared to scrutinize very closely the matters contained in a proposed law, they are not carrying out the duties they were sent here to perform. As a member of the house, who has not as yet given any expression of opinion which way I shall vote, I resent the implication that if I were to vote against the proposal to export power I should be part of a "cabal" in this chamber opposed to the Ontario government. I am not taking my orders from Ontario. I am not prepared, as the expression goes, to be a Charlie McCarthy for anyone. If I have opinions to express I am going to express them according to the light in which I see them, and I am not to be intimidated by statements made in this chamber by any other hon. member.

Electric Power Export
The hon. member who spoke so vehemently this afternoon was extremely anxious to throw innuendoes against other hon. members. Will he tell us that he was not within recent times closely associated with some of these private power interests in the province of Quebec. We know it; and yet he is so free with his own statements thrown across the floor of the house. I am not holding this against him in the least, but when he makes such statements he should be careful to have behind him the necessary accuracy.
I am prompted to say a word or two in this debate not because I want to discuss the merits or demerits of the bill with respect to the export of power; but when I made a statement in reference to the appointment of Doctor Hogg to the position of chairman of the hydro commission, I did so because I know something about Doctor Hogg's actions and his associations. It is common knowledge, and if I had time, if I had known that the hon. member was going to raise the question, I could have brought forward facts to prove that Doctor Hogg has been closely associated with private power interests in Canada. He has been their consulting engineer on many occasions, having made reports to private corporations on the question of private or public ownership, when the one or the other had to be brought into question.
I do not think this discussion is in order. The Chairman has shown a great deal of latitude in allowing this question to be discussed in committee, and I do not know where the debate will end. I would have been more content to discuss the clause introduced this afternoon and to keep strictly within the terms of section 4, and the amendment introduced by the Prime Minister, with which I am in agreement. Perhaps it offers more control to the governor in council and to parliament than we formerly had. because under the provisions as they stand it might be difficult to get a clear-cut interpretation. There might be a question of conflicting jurisdiction. My main purpose now, however, is to protest vigorously against the sort of speech that we have been compelled to listen to this afternoon.

It is not my desire to speak provocatively or with acrimony, and, indeed, I did not intend to speak at all at this time. However, I wish to discuss some of the safeguards that are contemplated in section 4 of this bill and in the amendment. But before I do so, I should like to make one or two observations. After listening to the hon. member for Winnipeg North I recall that not
so very long ago he made certain remarks as to how members on this side of the house were kept in line on government measures. If I remember rightly-and I am speaking from recollection-the hon. gentleman suggested that they were to be kept in line by having a judgeship, or a senatorship, or something of that land held dangling before them. I recall also the remarks made the other night with regard to the lobby that had been carried on in connection with, strange to say, a private bill which was not before the house. At the time I resented those remarks and I felt grateful to the Minister of Justice for stating that, in his opinion, those on this side could be trusted to use their good judgment and their common sense in connection with a matter of this kind. I thank him for that statement.
I think I am entitled to say here that throughout this whole discussion of the bill before us, and of any contemplated private bill which may be brought in, no living soul except members of the house-not the hon. member who spoke a short while ago, the member for Parry Sound-has ever asked me, or suggested directly or indirectly anything about what I would do in connection with the export of power from Ontario. Perhaps I have not the ability to carry out my determination; I gather from the remarks of my hon. friend opposite that nobody over here has. The only one who has that ability is the hon. member for Winnipeg North. I did wish, however, to see what the safeguards were that were being put around the private bill which was to be brought in.
Coming now to section 4, as I understand it, the safeguards which are being provided are to take care of the vital interests of this nation. Safeguards, I agree, are essential. My home town is one that has grown up by. and has been associated with, * hydro-electric energy, where the water from lake Superior falls to the lake Huron level; and our whole history has been closely linked with water power development. I mention this to illustrate some particulars in which I believe there should be safeguards in a bill such as the one we have before us. Every few years increased power has been required, and I have seen personally the effect of the development of industry on the surplus power available, pressing upon those owning the power to use their influence and make contacts so as to bring in industries which would make use of that power.
There are two essentials in regard to which there should be safeguards. In the first place there should be a definite determination and
Electric Power Export

incentive to use all power and to find uses for it in the dominion and particularly in the locality where the power is developed. Different standards have to be considered, depending upon the question whether the control is by private interests seeking profit or by public or quasi-public ownership bodies whose duty and trust are to the people at large. There is a distinct difference there.
In Sault Ste. Marie we have a public utilities commission which has been operating for years. The chairman has the absolute confidence of the people of Sault Ste. Marie, and the other members of the commission are similarly trusted. I mention this because it touches closely some considerations that have been brought forward in the house in connection with the bill now before us, although referable to the anticipated private bill in connection with the export of power from Ontario. There we have this situation. They are under obligation to take from a private power company an extra block of power; but it is optional; they do not have to pay for it until they take it. That power company have to carry that extra power and it is a dead loss to them unless they can make use of it. They have off-peak power, surplus power, a portion of which they have to supply to the city on demand, and having no use for it now they supply it for use under the boilers of the paper industry in Sault Ste. Marie. They supply at least a portion of that power. If the public utility commission had to take that power and pay for it, they would be in a similar position to the hydroelectric commission, in that they would have to pay for power for which they had no use. In view of the desire expressed by some hon. members to see that surplus power is kept for Canadian use, I would have every confidence that the chairman of that commission would do everything possible to develop uses for that power in and around that community first, and I would be content to allow them to export any remaining surplus across the line at Sault Ste. Marie, under the safeguards contemplated by this bill.
Another point on which I wish to touch for a moment is the danger of setting up vested interests in the United States with a right to look to a continuation of the supply of power. In the supplementary white paper the memorandum attached to the letter of the Secretary of State refers to the danger of United States industries becoming dependent upon imported power, and indicating what it would mean if the supply were cancelled. They would have to revert hastily to additional steam plant construction for base load power. I confess that to my mind this has been a serious danger. But in no
(Mr. Hamilton.]
provocative or acrimonious sense I want to read a statement which goes back to 1911. I was not very old then, but I carry forward even now some recollection of what was then said to be a very serious threat if we dealt with the United States of America. I want to follow that thought for a moment, because I think safeguards on that point are important. I quote from page 173 of the Canadian Annual Review, 1911, some remarks of the then Mr. R. L. Borden with reference to the 1911 election and the contemplated reciprocity agreement:
If we attempt the experiment of linking arms with our gigantic neighbour he will have something to say about the unlinking. Already we hear the astonishing suggestion that as congress has ratified this agreement Canada dare not refuse to do it. Against the vested interests of hundreds of millions, against the tremendous power and influence of gigantic trusts, in the face of the delicate and difficult international conditions created by the treaty, and confronted with a threatened dislocation of business infinitely greater than that which brought our government to its knees last year, Canada would be as capable of withdrawing, without consent, from this agreement as the fly from the spider's web.
That was in 1911, and I have heard here in the last two weeks some arguments that concerned me as those did then. But since 1911 we have changed our viewpoint as to the danger of trade entanglements or alliances or treaties with the United States, and the successors of the party which then took that extreme view, were in 1934 and 1935 seeking to bring about a trade agreement with the United States.

The point at issue in 1911 was the danger of trade moving in volume north and south, the danger that once we had entered into an agreement we would not be able to break it without creating international difficulty, the same argument that is advanced now. And I understand the reason why the right hon. leader of the opposition in 1934 did not make an agreement with the United States was that he could not make those channels deeper than they were and more binding than the United States was willing to make them, in other words, increasing the very danger which in 1911 we were warned against.
I wish to give as an illustration a situation which is of vital importance not only to my constituency but to Canada, in which the identical argument would apply. This is an iron and steel age. Practically our whole civilized life is based on iron and steel. Yet not one pound of iron ore, upon which that

great industry is dependent, is mined in Canada. The ore which comes into central Canada comes from the United States of America, from resources which are not inexhaustible, which are being depleted rather speedily. The hon. member for Davenport a year or two ago pointed out in this house that very danger. It is a very real one. To-day we in this country are utterly dependent for raw material for that great basic industry upon our neighbours across the line, whose resources of iron ore are being depleted with some speed. I confess I cannot see a great difference between the menace that confronts us if the United States should suddenly terminate those supplies and that which would arise if we were exporting hydroelectric energy to the United States and suddenly terminated that supply. As the memorandum to which I have referred suggests, what they would have to do would be to . resort to steam plants for their power. Similarly we would have to import ore from other countries, and probably pay more for it, as they would possibly have to pay more for power produced by coal burnt under boilers if that were necessary. I do not wish to detract at all from the seriousness of this question, but I do not think it applies with any greater seriousness to the export of hydro-electric energy than to other commodities which are exported.
The other day the hon. member for Davenport dealt with the diversion of water from the great lakes. To my mind that is on a different basis from hydro-electric energy, as in that case the United States have the physical control of .that diversion, which they have not in connection with hydro-electric energy going into their country.

I am not an electrician and do not profess to have much technical knowledge of electricity; but in connection with electricity I assume we could cut the wires or in other ways stop the exportation, which we cannot do in reference to the water being diverted at Chicago. So I do not think the illustration is altogether valid as an argument against allowing the exportation of hydroelectric energy.
In connection with section 4 we have the parliament of Canada or the governor in council acting for the people and having the say as to whether or not exports shall continue. Then we have other public utility bodies equally responsible to the people they represent. In my town they are responsible, among others, to the men and women out of work, to the people of that city, which is seeking for additional industries which would relieve the unemployment now prevailing. We should so surround our exportations that we do not make any misrepresentations or misleading statements. When dealing with a great nation at present on such friendly terms with Canada, in the words of the president can we not deal with them as neighbours; can we not make with that country an agreement such as an individual would make with his neighbour? It seems to me that at this time, when there is so .much suspicion and distrust, we should have faith and confidence in the relations that exist between nations. I may be talking foolishly and childishly, not as a man of the world; yet I am prepared to make these statements in any event. It is important that we should live up to the high standard of national and international conduct which is nowhere better exemplified than on the North American continent, where it has been an example to the world. So I think if we take care of these very real conditions that must be considered, with all the provisions that are embodied in this measure we shall be safeguarding the national interests of this dominion.

Mr. Chairman, while I
appreciate the wisdom of the suggestion of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, I simply cannot allow to go unchallenged the statement of the hon. member for Parry Sound to the effect that the Conservative party in this house was predisposed or had agreed to oppose the exportation of power from Canada. Coming from Ontario, and the particular district which I represent, I cannot allow such a statement to be made without a reply. So far as I am concerned- and I am sure I express the views of all my colleagues in the house-we have had a sincere desire to see this general bill dealing with the exportation of electric power so drafted that the interests of all parties in this country would be safeguarded, irrespective of whether the applicant for permission to export electric power should be the hydroelectric commission, or any quasi-public ownership enterprise, or a private concern.
I am willing to give a good deal more weight to the views and opinion of the hon. member for Parry Sound on the subject of remote control leadership than I am to his attitude towards the federal Conservative party. No member in this house is in a better position to have a knowledge of remote control leadership than the hon. member for Parry Sound. If we could believe the press of Ontario, for two years prior to 1934 the hon. gentleman was the constant companion of a remote control Liberal leader in Ontario, the present premier of that province.
The hon. member for Parry Sound says that one would think the export of power was something new. Oh, no, it is not. It is because of the expei'ience we have had with the resultant effects of the export of power that individual members of this party and the Conservative party in this house have been endeavouring to see that amendments were included in the bill now before us. It is because we have learned that renewals are not precedents, as the hon. gentleman would seem to think, for the granting of new applications. It is because we have learned from experience that once an application is granted, unless it is surrounded with the strictest terms, a vested right is created, and you must have an excellent reason for refusing the renewal because of the international complications which arise therefrom. It is because of our experiences at Massena and in regard to the Chicago drainage canal and the export of power at Niagara Falls, which were detailed by the hon. member for Daven-
port, that we have learned that care must be exercised in granting new licences for the export of power from Canada.
May I say to the hon. member for Parry Sound that as far as I am concerned, and as far as most of the members of the Conservative party in this house to my knowledge are concerned, if the hon. gentleman or any other hon. member introduces a private bill now or in the future providing for the export of power from this country he will find that we will consider that problem not from the point of view of whether it is the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario. not from the point of view of whether it is a private corporation, but from the point of view of what is in the national interests of the people of Canada as a whole. That and none other will be the governing factor.

We have had the
pleasure-and such apparently it was to many hon. members opposite-of listening to a high class speech by the hon. member for Parry Sound. He spoke in such slighting terms of the language used by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe that one would have expected that at least he would use what might be called language consistent with the amenities of civilized society. But it was ovaltine, a chocolate bar, and street-car tickets; this from a member of the legal profession, who gave a learned opinion in connection with the MacLaren bond issue, and who rises in his place in this house as an exemplar of. all that is fit and proper in the conduct of public business. That is his language. That is the language of one who asserts himself as a leader of the bar in his province. I believe he is now-well, I am reminded that he was-a bencher of the law society of Ontario. The language he used here to-day is as I have indicated-and he holds himself up now to this house as an example. One would expect at least that the language used would not be of the kind he condemns. But he has seen fit to condemn in one breath and to approve in the other, using himself the language to which I have referred. I am accustomed to abuse; that is nothing new. There is, of course, an old saying that when you have a bad case you should abuse the attorney on the opposite side. I make no complaint about that; but I do make this complaint-not on behalf of myself, for I have not complained personally-that those who set themselves up as examples and condemn in such vigorous terms the language said to have been used by the hon. member

Electric Power Export
for Dufferin-Simcoe should not themselves sink to what they describe as an improper level, by using the language we have heard.
Something has been said about a lobby. I spoke about the dangers of lobbies with respect to private legislation. I in no sense indicated that any member of this house was lobbying. I spoke of what I said in parliament-I believe it was during the second session in which I enjoyed a place in it-at a time when the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, Mr. W. F. Nickle and I on the last day of the session joined in as vigorous a denouncement as we were capable of making of the lobby that was carried on in respect to the Bank Act. We were not in any sense denouncing the lobby of members of the house by members of the house-far from it. We were pointing out that systematic lobbies were being maintained by members of the legal profession on behalf of great interests concerned; that they were buttonholing members in the corridors and suggesting that they give support to this measure, to that clause or that paragraph of a bill.
What is more, we did something to end it. Every private bill is a conflict of interest against usage. Everyone knows that a private bill is an effort to have a majority of the members of parliament make an exception in favour of an interest. Whether it be a divorce bill or any other measure, it matters not; it is the interest that is the controlling factor. I pointed that out the other day, as I did twenty-five years ago in this chamber, when we denounced the practice of interests concerned employing a high type of lawyers who were buttonholing and lobbying members of parliament to support their views.
I read in the paper the other day that the Ontario government had engaged the services of two Ottawa lawyers for the purpose of lobbying their interests here. The presence of one of them in the debate in this house during the progress of the bill has always been apparent. There is no questioning the fact that lobbying has been discussed in every democratic parliament of the world, and the danger of it is apparent to every man who believes that democracy could be set aside lightly by efforts such as that. If hon. members refer to Hansard they will find what was said with respect to lobbying on the occasion I have mentioned. No one suggested that any member was lobbying any other member. It was for the first time indicated to the house that the hon. member for Parry Sound was to have charge of the private bill, and he suggests that some fellow member was endeavouring to lobby me with a glass of ovaltine or a chocolate bar,
and the hon. member for Kootenay East with a street-car ticket. To that level has debate descended this afternoon.
Whatever else may be said with respect to the note received yesterday, and laid before the house, at least it vindicates the position taken by some of us with respect to this legislation. At page 13 of the white paper laid on the table to-day, the Secretary of State for the United States uses these words:
It is well known that successive governments in Canada have been traditionally reluctant to permit the long term exportation of power to the United States. The principal reasons underlying this policy were concisely stated in a letter, recently made public, from the premier of Ontario to the Minister of Trade and Commerce at Ottawa. The objections, as therein stated, were as follows:
1.	That the exportation of power results in the establishment in the United States of dependent communities or industries.
2.	That irrespective of the terms of the agreement under which export delivery is made, the commitments become irrevocable; that is, the deliveries cannot be suspended or terminated at any later date without giving rise to international complications and being regarded as an unfriendly act.
3.	That the export of power enables industries, which otherwise would establish themselves or branches thereof in Canada, to handle their Canadian business from factories located in the United States.
It must be clear to all who have given thought to the problem that those reasons which have in the past made the exportation of power undesirable from the point of view of Canada have made the importation of power undesirable from the point of view of the United States. In the case of the latter, a broad policy of national defence is also involved. On this aspect of the question, it is perhaps sufficient merely to say that many of the industries most necessary to the life of a nation in times of national emergency require very large and uninterrupted supplies of power. The fact that the government of the United States anticipates no such emergency does not relieve it of the responsibility of taking the possibility into account.
And then follows this:
While sympathizing with the desires of Ontario and Quebec, the government of the United States considers that its primary obligation is to view the problem in terms of protection for the general power market in the United States and for those American industries which might become dependent upon imported supplies of power. In this connection, it may be pointed out that if the Northeastern power market in the United States were to become dependent for any considerable portion of its power supply upon withdrawable imports, it would be faced with the constant danger of having to revert hastily to additional steam plant construction for base load power.
In the circumstances, the government of the United States believes that it would be failing to discharge its proper obligations if it were to give its consent to the importation of hydroelectric power, even on a temporary basis,

without simultaneously providing for the development of an alternative and equally economical domestic supply to be available when the imported power was withdrawn.
There is a concise statement of the considered policy of the United States of America, not only with respect to electric power, but also with respect to every matter that affects its national well-being, namely the protection of United States interests and industries.
When I heard the hon. member for Parry Sound speak of the tremendous friendliness of the United States for Canada, I could not but remember that only a few months ago, in 1935, this dominion signed a trade agreement with the United States, and that within a few months thereafter a revenue tax of three cents a pound was placed upon animal fats, thereby destroying the lard industry in this country, so far as price was concerned. Why? Because they were carrying out the policies that Mr. Secretary Hull has now enunciated in this note to the Dominion of Canada. During the past few weeks there passed the House of Representatives a bill that places against Canadian pork products a duty of six cents a pound. This is a prohibitive duty, and if it goes into effect it will prevent the sending of a single pound of pork products into the United States. That bill is now pending before the United States senate. Mr. Secretary Hull believes it to be the first duty of every government to care for its own people and its own country. He has indicated in no fulsome flattery and in no platitudinous discussion that that is so. He is a realist and his government is realistic. It considers the first duty of government is to care for the material, spiritual, and, shall I say the social well-being of its people.
I should like to remind the committee that the first comprehensive proposals made to the United States of America for a trading agreement came, not from a Liberal government but from a Conservative government. I say this now so that there may be no misunderstanding about it. The Conservative party never was the author of the statement, "No more trade or truck with the Yankees." Who was it said that? I ask the hon. member for Parry Sound who was the author of that?

The hon. member for Al-goma West has asked a question. Let me tell him that no proposal was made by the Conservative government for trading with the United States until we had concluded trade agreements within the empire. Why? Because we knew that in Great Britain there existed a stable market for our agricultural products. We knew that there we would not have the fluctuations in policy brought about by the changing tariff views of the one party as compared with the other. We know now that to-day we have republican tariff in the United States of America. We know that it is the highest tariff in the history of the United States. We know that the president can negotiate trade agreements only if goods now dutiable are not made free and the tariff is not reduced by more than fifty per cent. To-day the average ad valorem tariff of the United States is nearer fifty per cent than forty per cent. If you include the specific duties, the average is sixty per cent. Half of sixty per cent is thirty per cent, so that the only tariff we can secure from our great neighbours is one of thirty per cent, and that is called a low tariff.

Mr. Speaker, the government is taking no exception to this bill. It does not make any drastic change, but I think the sponsor has in mind that in eases where new developments spring up, and there is a possibility of a certain portion of the power being exported, the company or individual promoting the measure shall come to parliament and obtain a private bill for that purpose. With that suggestion, the government has no quarrel; indeed I think I may say on behalf of the government that we will go even a step further. Those were not the words of the Conservative party; they are the words of the spokesman of the right hon. gentleman who now leads the government. That hon. gentleman spoke for the government when he said they would go even a step further than the hon. member for Leeds. He said:

As Mr. Secretary Hull points out, all governments have been opposed to long term contracts for power. It may well be that over

I would only suggest that when the Minister of Justice is considering the terms of the amendment which he has read, it might be well to make it clear that the conditions imposed by the licence shall be the conditions which will apply to any private act.
The Prime Minister very properly used the argument, why not depend upon the private act? But the reason we should not depend upon the private act is that the terms of the licence which will be obtained by those companies whose licences are to be renewed from time to time contain these provisions, and they are part of the general conditions that govern the whole situation. Therefore the general bill, namely the enabling act, should contain like conditions. I suggest that because I regard one or two of them as being tremendously important. There is, for instance, the one that deals with the

I mention this, Mr. Chairman, without going further into the matter, because I should like to make it abundantly clear that, in opposing the general position in respect to power export there was nothing in it that had to do in any way, shape or form with immediate conditions; there was no effort to arouse animosity against the government of Ontario. To suggest that thirty-eight or thirty-nine persons were so powerful as to be able to effect this purpose does violence to my understanding of the weight of the thirty-eight persons. To suggest that it can be done involves, in my judgment, the negation of the very theory upon which government by majority rests. But we have followed the traditional policy of this party; we have followed the traditional policy of the Liberal party as declared in this house, the unanimous view, as the Prime Minister was at pains to point out the other day, as expressed on more than one occasion; and it was for that reason that we are opposed to the export of power. I submit that beyond all peradventure, if the amendments which have been suggested, amplified by the one that was just read, being, as I submit with deference, broadened so as to cover the conditions to which I refer, were passed, we would then in the enabling act have indicated to all the general conditions which will govern hereafter the granting of a private act; and, more, we would have maintained that position which the Prime Minister took in 1928, the position which was taken by the late administration, and the position which has been taken by the government of to-day; for there has been no departure that I know of or that any other hon. member has heard of that changes the general attitude of mind of successive governments towards the question of long term export of power. This was the Liberal principle declared time after time in Ontario and elsewhere in Canada.
But it is not necessary to go that far. All one needs to do is to take the statement made on behalf of the government of the day in February, 1928. By that we have stood. If in doing so we have created a cabal; if by doing so we have trodden upon the toes of a new Liberal policy of which we were not advised; if there is a new one in the offing of which we have no knowledge, yet indeed we can say with the greatest consistency that we have maintained the unani-

subtopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927, CHAPTER 95
speechtext:
It is with a sense of deep responsibility that I rise tonight to take part in this debate. I am quite aware that British parliamentary custom has decided that the whips of the two parties should take very little part in debate. While I am simply deputy whip and act only on occasion, nevertheless I do from time to time take the place of the chief government whip,

and therefore I recognize that responsibility in rising to discuss this bill to-night. Were it not for the circumstances surrounding the particular measure now before the house I would not be on my feet. It is my intention to make as sure as I can that no word of mine shall hurt the feelings of any member of this house, and I trust also that nothing will be said which will be even provocative.
There are several matters deeply related to the question under discussion in connection with the two bills that have been introduced purporting to amend the Immigration Act and the Chinese Immigration Act, but I do not intend to deal with these related questions. Rather I shall confine myself to questions embedded in the measures themselves.
The question brought before us by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) is one of deep significance to the province of British Columbia. It is one which, if left unaltered in its present status, will soon be of vital concern to the dominion as a whole. I know the people of western Canada fairly well, and there is one thing that the people of British Columbia require of their public men more perhaps than any other attribute. It is that when any deep and embarrassing question arises, the people of that province shall know where their representatives stand, and out of deference to and in appreciation of that feeling on the part of the people of British Columbia, I state at this point that if these two bills before the house are forced to the conclusion of a vote, I shall vote against the second reading of both. Having so declared myself, I shall later on take the extreme liberty, with whatever force is at my command, of recommending to the proposer of these bills, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, that in the interests of British Columbia, in the interests of the very object which he has in mind and for which he has been working in and out of parliament for fifteen years or more, he withdraw them so that in the circumstances in which parliament finds itself at the present time it will not be necessary to vote the bills down.

speechtext:
I do not wish to get into any altercation with the hon. gentleman over a question of order, but the only difference between the two bills is that one purports to amend the Chinese Immigration Act and the other purports to amend the Immigration Act.
Japanese Immigration

It is not possible properly to discuss, from the standpoint of British Columbians, the question of the exclusion of Japanese, through any instrument whatever, without discussing everything that arises from immigration and, therefore, from the policies adopted by this parliament to conduct and to regulate immigration.
As I was saying, I intend to suggest to the hon. member that in the very interests of the object he has in mind these bills should not be pressed to a vote during this session. Later on, I shall give my reasons for that suggestion. It is my intention also to show to the best of my ability why I think it is absolutely necessary for me, coming from British Columbia and having a sense of the responsibility that rests upon a member of this house, to vote against the bill on this occasion. Further I intend as well as I can, and even at the expense of repeating some of the arguments that have been made, to put forward some of the reasons why I believe that sooner or later action must be taken to bring about that which these bills purport to accomplish. That action must of necessity be taken.
Two results have followed from the discussion that has taken place upon the hon. member's motion. One is that this government has already set up machinery which we sincerely hope will bring to light in what degree, if any, illegal entries have been made from Asiatic countries, with particular reference perhaps to the race mentioned in Bill No. 11. There has been set up-or rather enlarged, for I understand it was set up previously-another investigating committee which will act more or less in conjunction with the board of review that is dealing entirely with illegal entrance and the steps necessary to be taken immediately to stop it, but the interdepartmental committee acting in conjunction with that board will inquire, I take it, into the whole question of Asiatic immigration.

May I ask the hon. member a question? Has there been any change since the announcement made by the Prime Minister on March 7? He was asked by the leader of the opposition about these boards of inquiry, and his answer was, as reported at page 1066 of Hansard:
Mr. Mackenzie King:	The board has been
appointed to deal with the subject of illegal entries-
