Then he goes on to say:
However, I would assume that in any inquiry directed to illegal entries much information that was incidental thereto would be ascertained.

Is the hon. member suggesting that there is to be another board, or that this board is to go further than the statement of the Prime Minister indicated?

subtopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927, CHAPTER 95
speechtext:
I do not want to be unkind to the hon. member, for whom I have great personal regard; but if he paid more attention to the answers given by ministers of the crown he would not have had to ask me that question, because he will find on Hansard an answer to his own question, where the Prime Minister said that this interdepartmental committee was set up and is separate entirely from the board of review, whose function is confined to the question of illegal entry. This interdepartmental committee I take it has upon it representatives not only of the Department of Immigration but of the Department of Labour and the Department of National Defence. Perhaps one should not say that too loudly, but these two departments are represented on that committee, which is inquiring into every question relating to oriental immigration into Canada, which, of course, means largely into British Columbia.	.
A second benefit has resulted from the introduction of this bill by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. Oftentimes the position of British Columbia in the general scheme of things Canadian is misunderstood. For long years the position of that far western province with respect to all questions relating to immigration has been misunderstood. But I take it from this debate, and especially from the words used by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and other ministers, as well as by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), that now our position is better understood than it has been at any previous time in the history of this question.
What is the situation? I have before me two orders in council passed under authority of the Immigration Act. One is P.C. 2115 dated September 16, 1930, which puts a prohibition upon the entry into Canada, except of course with certain exceptions, of immigrants from Asiatic countries, though it clearly sets out that it is not concerned and does not deal with any Asiatic nation with which Canada has a treaty or convention. Then there is another order in council, which was referred to the other night, P.C. 695, dated March 21, 1931, and amended April 23. 1937. This order in council deals with steps taken to prohibit immigration of any kind into Canada, again with certain exceptions. The exceptions are: Those who come from Great Britain with sufficient funds to maintain themselves until they have opportunity to secure employment; those who come from

Japanese Immigration
the United States with sufficient funds, and agriculturists with sufficient funds to go into the business of farming. In this order in council there is also a proviso as regards immigrants as defined in paragraph 2, that is, those entering from the United States, and immigrants as defined in paragraph 4, that is, agriculturists who have sufficient means to farm in Canada: " Provided that these are destined for settlement in a province which has not signified its disapproval of such immigration." There is a clear recognition of the principle that, largely because of conditions in Canada to-day, persons to be admitted to this country must be destined for a province which has not signified objection to their entry.
I do not need to point out that immigrants from Asiatic countries who come to Canada come only to British Columbia. The general principle underlying these prohibitions is this, that because of the situation in which labour finds itself, because of the competition with which those who are farming may be faced, because of general competition in labour or in other means of gaining a livelihood in Canada, it is not right to permit immigrants to enter the country. Yet we find that immigration from Asiatic countries is concentrated in British Columbia and is of such a kind that it utterly displaces all other labour with which it comes in contact. That is a situation which cannot be denied and to which I call attention on behalf of British Columbia.
Ordinarily immigration is stopped because of its effect on labour and those engaged in production. In British Columbia we find two results from the immigration policies of Canada. One is that in those parts of the province in which Asiatic settlement is concentrated labour is ousted, farm values lowered very materially, and rural credit lessened and in some places destroyed. What else do we find as a result of the general immigration policies of Canada? My eyes are turned now to that great area of country running from Vancouver north clear through the centre of British Columbia for practically a thousand miles, a country containing the richest mineral section imaginable, from which untold millions of dollars have been taken, but which as yet in many places has been hardly touched and is still open for exploration. In that country we find seven or eight settlements, many of them isolated, several of them finding it impossible to maintain contact with each other because of lack of transportation. In that country there is everything to support a larger population- diversified farming, cattle, hogs, wheat and everything one can think of. It extends both
east and west of the mountains. It is traversed by the great valley of the Fraser river and all its tributaries, and from east to west it is crossed by the Peace river waterway, with all its tributaries. Yet we find that because of lack of population that country is not in a position to support itself. It has over seven hundred miles of Canadian National railway lines, owned by the government of Canada. In another direction it is crossed by 450 miles of the Pacific Great Eastern railway, which is owned by the province of British Columbia. Every mile of railway line within that area is owned by the taxpayers; yet because it is without immigrants who should be going in there, the railways are unable to operate except at a terrific loss, though they are running through one of the richest parts of Canada.
The situation is this:	British Columbia,
surfeited on the one hand with Asiatic immigration, is crying and demanding that steps be taken at the earliest possible moment to see what can be done with the government of Great Britain in order to bring to this portion of the province immigrants properly directed, properly financed, properly organized and carefully selected. The province wants them. Only yesterday at Victoria the city of Prince George presented to the Rowell commission a submission in connection with immigration from the British Isles, and that plea for British immigration is not divorced from the question of oriental immigration. During the last few months a new and, if you wish, strange doctrine in international relations has been proclaimed by some great states. The doctrine is that parent states are responsible for the welfare and entitled to direct the destiny of strong minorities of their people who live in foreign states. It is true that up to the present time this refers only to states contiguous to what are called the parent states; but in the western part of Canada we have an Asiatic people migrating to British Columbia, with nothing between Canada and the country from which these people come except the Pacific ocean. With the transportation facilities of to-day the Pacific ocean is hardly a greater barrier than an ordinary boundary line between nations.
I do not point out these things simply that the government should take cognizance of them because, as I said in the beginning, I realize that already cognizance has been taken of the situation in British Columbia. Having said so much, however, may I just take a few minutes more to state why I cannot vote for this bill. I realize the importance of the measure brought into the house
Japanese Immigration

by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, and I should like to read some remarks made during the course of this debate by the leader of the opposition, for whom it goes without saying I have the highest respect. Mind you, these words were spoken by the right hon. gentleman, who was quite aware of the. responsibility that attached to him through his past experience as Prime Minister and Minister of External Affairs, and who knows the delicate touch with which questions of this kind must be handled even in times of peace. The right hon. gentleman said:
On the other hand, not for a moment would I pass the bill in its present forai. Without placing a time limit as to when it should come into force, or providing that it should become effective by proclamation, I think we would be courting a very serious situation indeed, and one which we could not contemplate at this particular moment, having regard to our earnest desire to keep our own country out of the conflict in Asia.
These are not idle words; they are the words of the leader of the opposition who, as I said, was speaking from the depths of experience. Later on he said:
Therefore, while I should like to commend the hon. member who introduced the measure to the house, and hope that the government are prepared to accept the principle of it, I am one of those who, accepting that measure and believing strongly in it, would not for a moment urge its passing in its present form, as I believe it would be a very dangerous thing for us to do at this time.
I know there are men around me who feel that it is perhaps an exaggeration to point out the difficulties and embarrassments which might arise by reason of any action taken in connection with the exclusion of an Asiatic race from our country, but here are the words of the right hon. gentleman, who says not only that such action is dangerous but that it should not be taken if we are really earnest in our desii'e to keep this country out of the conflict which is now raging in the orient.
In the last twelve or fifteen years we have gone very far in our relations with the British Empire. We have taken such steps and have declared ourselves from time to time in such manner that the Statute of Westminster of a few years ago was, after all, only a manifestation of that great development which has taken place in Canada. But this I ask the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and those newspapers in British Columbia which have been commenting rather bitterly upon the hesitancy shown by parliament in passing this measure: While it is right that we should become masters in our own home; while it is right that in matters relating to defence

we should cut ourselves off from external influence; while undoubtedly it is right that we should decide that our destiny along the pathway of the world should be cleaved only by ourselves, have we reached the time when we can forget what has been the relationship in the past between this country and the British Empire? Have we reached the time when we can pay no attention to the call of kinship? The Prime Minister pointed out, in words that must be heeded by anyone who heard or read them, that in Japan there is a deliberate effort designed to break down the friendly relations which in the past have existed between Japan and the British Empire. If there were in Canada, or in any part of the world, some fiendish mind which wished to make certain that if anything were to happen by way of a world conflagration Canada should be in it, is there anything that such a fiendish mind could conceive which would be more likely to attain its objective than so to arrange matters that the one final spark which brought about a world crisis should be an overt act on the part of Canada, committed by this parliament?
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni, having been satisfied, as he must be, with the discussion which has taken place, and filled, as I know he is, with the desire to relieve British Columbia of its Asiatic problem; realizing that if the suggestions of the leader of the opposition were taken-and the hon. member agreed to accept them the other night-that nothing could be done in any event within a year and a half or two years; that in that time Canada will have gone ahead with a reconsideration of its whole immigration problem, and that she may be making extra relations with the British Isles concerning immigration under which, without offence being given, there might be an exclusion of Asiatics; and once more stating that I must vote against this measure if it comes to a vote, thereby showing the hon. member that I am not trying to save myself from embarrassment, with all the sincerity of which I am capable and with all the powers at my command, I ask him in the interests of British Columbia, in the interests of Canada and of all which he has at heart-a better, safer and wiser settlement of the Asiatic problem of British Columbia-seriously to consider the withdrawal of his bills.

Mr. Speaker, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) stated a few weeks ago, when the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) first brought his bill before the house, that it was one of the most important measures parliament would have

Japanese Immigration
to consider-particularly at this juncture in world affairs-he stated a fact which I believe appeals to the reason and judgment of every hon. member.
There is no doubt that the question on the Pacific coast is one of deep and vital concern. We have evidence of that in the restrained but definite speeches made by members from that province, and we see it also in the concern exhibited in Vancouver and on the Pacific coast generally in relation to this whole problem. I think, however, if we are to reach a sound decision on the merits of the bill we are now considering, it is necessary to take stock of all that would be implied in the house passing the measure.
The Japanese immigration question first became one of concern a great many years ago. Hon. members will recall that in 1894 the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland entered into a treaty, known as the United Kingdom-Japanese treaty, with the Kingdom of Japan. Canada gave adherence to that treaty. One of its provisions stated that the subjects of each party to the agreement should have full liberty to enter, travel or reside in any part of the dominions and possessions of the other. It was the freedom given in that provision which in the first instance led to the heavy Japanese immigration to the Pacific coast. To such an extent had that immigration increased that in the three years from 1905 to 1907 upwards of 12,000 Japanese came to Canada. Even then the matter was one of considerable concern to the Canadian people. The treaty I mentioned a moment ago, to which Canada had given adherence, was still in effect. It was that situation which led to the mission of the late Hon. Rodolphe Lemieux to Japan in 1907 to discuss with the Japanese government the question of limiting Japanese immigration to this country.
I should like to repeat that which was pointed out by the Prime Minister, namely that the Japanese government acted in a wholly reasonable manner at that time. An arrangement was reached by which Japanese immigration to Canada was limited to about 500 persons a year, and that arrangement, as was stated by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, remained in effect until after the termination of the treaty, which took place, as I now recall, in 1921.
The so-called gentleman's agreement negotiated by Hon. Mr. Lemieux continued in effect. It is quite true the matter was dis-51952-101
cussed in parliament in 1922 or 1923. In 1928 further representations were made to the Japanese government and further reductions in the migration to Canada were effected, bringing the number to 150 a year. I think it is only fair to say that the Japanese government have lived up to the gentleman's agreement of 1907 and the later understanding of 1928.

A feeling exists on the Pacific coast that a considerable number of Japanese have entered Canada illegally. The illegal entry of immigrants is not a new thing. When speaking to his bill the hon. member said that he did not intend it to deal with any except those who would come in under the gentleman's agreement. An interdepartmental committee was set up, as alluded to by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) which studied this question. Certain conclusions were arrived at among which was the one that we should deal only with those Japanese who might be in Canada illegally. When I was on the Pacific coast last summer, I was told that there were hundreds of Japanese who had entered the country illegally, and my hon. friend seems to harbour the same * thought. As a result of the work of this interdepartmental committee, a board of review was established this week in Vancouver. This board is made up of Doctor Keenleyside of the Department of External Affairs, Mr. Taylor, Superintendent of Immigration on the Pacific coast, and Inspector Fish of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

Every one on the Pacific coast who has a suspicion, or any knowledge, that a Japanese is in the country illegally, has been invited to present his information to the board, either personally or in writing. Any statement made to the board will be fully examined, and any Japanese found to be in Canada illegally will be deported. At the same time, it is only right to say that the Japanese who are legally in Canada will not be disturbed by the work of this board of review.

The other evening the hon. member for Comox-Alberni said that the reason the Chinese were dissatisfied with the action taken by Canada was because they felt they were discriminated against as compared with the Japanese. The

inference to be drawn from the hon. member's remarks was that if the Japanese were put in the same position as the Chinese, this objection on the part of the Chinese would largely disappear. A few years ago I had an opportunity of having a long discussion with an eminent Chinese gentleman, a man who, in his knowledge of languages, of history and of philosophy, stands in the front ranks in China. He was a man of great ability, and we discussed this particular question. He did not raise objection to the fact that we did not wish to have Chinese in Canada, but he did object to the manner in which we had gone about effecting this.
My hon. friend proposes to apply the same method to the Japanese. You cannot affront a proud people in this way. To Japan the question is not one of expediency but of principle. To her the mere fact that a few hundreds or thousands of her nationals will or will not be admitted to the dominions of other countries is immaterial, so long as no question of national susceptibilities is involved. The important question is whether Japan as a nation is or is not entitled to the proper respect and consideration of other nations. I shall take only a moment in order not to delay action by the house, as I wish to see a vote on this question to-night. There is a great deal of sympathy in Ontario for the people of British Columbia regarding oriental immigration. This is not only a domestic problem ; it is also imperial and it is international. On this question the people of Canada, I believe, think the same as those of New Zealand and Australia, that the time has come when this country should be a white man's country and further oriental immigration should be prohibited. We talk about gentlemen's agreements. Why in the world, when nobody pays any attention to treaties or pacts, should we expect that they are going to pay any attention to a gentleman's agreement? The people of the two industrial provinces are three thousand miles away from British Columbia; but I was out there in 1927 and I saw the way in which the oriental people are permeating every branch of business-lumbering, mining, and retail stores; these activities have been almost taken away from white men in that province, with the result that business men and the younger people who are coming from the schools and universities are finding it hard to make a living.
I would not say one word to offend Japan; far from it. I think the greatest mistake ever made was when, at Washington, to please the people of the United States we parted from the Japanese alliance. The British Empire never made a greater mistake. The mother country kept good order in the far east, and she arranged immigration policies so that New Zealand and Australia have remained white men's countries; there are no Japanese there. The same is largely true of the United States. Yet to please the people of the United States we parted from the Anglo-Japanese alliance. I think the government would be taking a step in the right direction if it adopted this measure. We want to see Canada as a whole, like the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, maintained as a white man's country.
Japanese Immigration

I congratulate the members from British Columbia upon their attitude. I believe their views on this question are those of the people of Canada. I am sorry that the old alliance was broken, and I can only hope that the government will not mistake any longer the babble of the pacifists for the voice of the Canadian people in either national or international affairs, and particularly in regard to this great domestic problem. Something must be done. Gentlemen's agreements are mere scraps of paper. Last year 101 Japanese came in and nearly all have stayed in British Columbia. In the case of the Chinese, sixty per cent remained in British Columbia and the rest have moved across Canada. The time has come when we shall not be violating any agreement if we take the action that has been proposed. What Great Britain has done with Japan for Australia and New Zealand can be done for the people of Canada. Japan has obtained room for expansion; she now has Manchuria and part of China; no longer does she need Canada for her surplus population.
I congratulate the mover of the bill. I hope it will be supported by every hon. member, because I believe the unanimous wish of the Canadian people is that in future Canada, like New Zealand and Australia, shall be a white man's country.

(2)	Subject to any regulation of the governor in council in that behalf, the governor in council may grant licences for the construction, placing or laying of any transmission line or line of wire or other conductor for the exportation of power, or of any pipe line or other like contrivance for the exportation of fluid.

They have had time for full consideration of it. My personal opinion was that without a declaration that transmission lines or lines of wire or other conductors for the exportation of power, and all pipe lines and other like contrivances for the exportation of fluid from any place in Canada to any place outside of Canada are works for the general advantage of Canada, this parliament would be deprived of jurisdiction over such lines, and any regulation made with respect to such lines, as was provided in subsection 2 of section 6 of the bill, would be invalid. I quite understand that this is declaring works to be constructed in future to be works for the general advantage of Canada, but I think it advisable for parliament to make that declaration. And with all respect I think such a declaration is within the competence of parliament. There are a number of cases to which one might refer, but I do not intend to refer to them to-night. We have made a similar declaration in the Railway Act. Parliament has declared that lines of railway

which come in contact with lines which are already lines for the general advantage of Canada thereby become lines for the general advantage of Canada. That is a declaration relating to works to be constructed in the future, and I think that if the one is valid, the proposed declaration is also valid.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: TRANSFER TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext:
The
Department of Justice advises against the amendment proposed by my hon. friend. Of course, as he knows, this section 6 merely proposes to change the place where what was already in the old act will be found in the future. There is no change at all except to place the section in another part of the bill. Since 1907 this has been the law of Canada, and it has never been challenged.
That is only to initiate what I have to say. Section 92 of the British North America Act, item 10, which gives jurisdiction to provincial legislatures, reads as follows:
10. Local works and undertakings other than such as are of the following classes:
These are the exceptions:
a. Lines of steam or other ships, railways, canals, telegraphs, and other works and undertakings connecting the province with any other or others of the provinces, or extending beyond the limits of the province:
This is the item on which we base our contention that it is within the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada. In the case of Hewson v. Ontario Power Company, 36 Supreme Court Reports, page 596, the question was as to the validity of a dominion incorporating act which gave power to the company to connect its wires with the wires of an electricity company in the United States. It was held that the subject matter of the charter was obviously not a local one, and that therefore it was valid by reason of this item 10a of section 92. This has always been the view of the Department of Justice. I find that on November 14, 1933, the deputy minister of justice, with the concurrence of the minister, the Hon. Mr. Guthrie, advised the deputy minister of the interior that the power works and appurtenant transmission lines constructed by the Calgary Power Company constituted, by reason of the manner in which they are interconnected and operated for the distribution of power, works and undertakings connecting the province of Alberta with other provinces and therefore are subject to the exclusive legislative authority of the dominion parliament in virtue of the combined operation of section 91, item 29, and section 92, item 10a of the British North America Act.

That is, that they extended their lines into Saskatchewan.

speechtext:
Yes. Of course to accept the amendment offered by my hon. friend would imply a doubt as to the validity not only of what has been in the law with regard to the export of power since 1907, but in many other enactments which are the law of the country at the present time. This we are not willing to do. In addition to that, if the amendment of my hon. friend is needed; if it would remove any doubt as to the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada in the matter, we submit that it should be done in the private bills when they come, and not in this public bill.
My hon. friend has referred to the section in the Railway Act which purports to give jurisdiction by saying that certain railways are for the general advantage of Canada. But that very section has been submitted to the courts, and in the case of Luscar Collieries Limited v. McDonald et al, reported in 1925 Supreme Court Reports, page 460, the majority of the court found that this section is invalid.

subtopic: TRANSFER TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext: Which section?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: TRANSFER TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext:
That section in the Railway Act to which my. hon. friend has referred. This declaration that works for the general advantage of Canada would come under paragraph c. of item 10 of section 92, which reads:
(c) Such works as, although wholly situate within the province, are before or after their execution declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces.
The majority of the supreme court found that this paragraph could not be used in a general way to cover general works in the future which are not specified. It applies to works already executed or to be executed, and which are especially defined and described. Here is what Mr. Justice Duff said, at page 476:
The grounds on which it can be argued that section 6 (c) of the Railway Act does not constitute a valid declaration within section 92, 10(c) of the British North America Act, can be very concisely stated. The object of this provision, it is said, was not to enable the dominion to take away jurisdiction from the provinces in respect of a given class of potential works; works, that is to say, which are not in existence, which may never come into existence, and the execution of which is not in contemplation; the purpose of the provision is rather to enable the dominion to assume control over specific existing works, or works the execution of which is in contemplation. The control intended to be vested in the dominion is the control over the execution of the work and over the executed work. If a
declaration in respect of all works comprised within a generic description be competent, the necessary consequence would appear to be that, with regard to the class of works designated by the description, provincial jurisdiction would be excluded, although dominion jurisdiction might never be exercised, and although no work answering the description should ever come into existence. In support of this view it may be said that the purport of the declaration authorized appears to be that the work which is the subject of it either is an existing work, beneficial to the country as a whole, or is such a work as ought to be executed, or, at all events, is to be executed, in the interests	of	the	country	as awhole. An affirmation in general terms, for example, an affirmation that all railways owned or operated hereafter by dominion company are works which ought to be or will be executed, as beneficial	to	the	country	as a
whole, would be almost, if not quite, meaningless. and could hardly have been contemplated as the basis of jurisdiction.
This was the finding of the majority of the supreme court. I think the declaration, suggested by my hon. friend would be quite in place in a private bill authorizing the export of power, say	by	the	hydro-electriccommission of Ontario, at a certain place. But the work has to be either executed or contemplated, and while this amendment is really generic in its scope, I submit that we would do better not	to	enact it in	connection with this bill.

speechtext: In reply to the right hon. gentleman, in the first place I submit that the opinion of Mr. Justice Duff in the case cited is rather in support of the contention I now make instead of being against it. In the act as it stands at present there is section 8, that is, in the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act, chapter 54 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927. It is there. I think it has never been enforced. It is true that there has been regulation as to the place at which the line crosses the boundary, and, in some instances, some regulation as to the crossing of the boundary, but that is not the full purport of the new subsection 2 of section 6 of this bill. Let me read this new subsection:
No person shall, without a licence, construct or place in position any line of wire or other
Electric Power Export

conductor or contrivance for the exportation of power or any pipe line or other like contrivance for the exportation of fluid.
That is a line for the exportation, of power. That means the line from the generating station or the power station or the transformer station through the province to the boundary and crossing the boundary, and it is that line, mentioned in the new subsection 2 of the bill, over which the government should have supervision and power of regulation. That provision is not within the power of parliament unless that line is previously declared to be a line for the general advantage of Canada.
My next point is in connection with section 8 of the existing act, which is subsection 3 as it now stands in my amendment, which states:
_ Subject to any regulations of the governor in council in that behalf, the governor in council may grant licences for the construction, placing or laying of any line of wire or other conductor for the exportation of power, or of any pipe line or other like contrivance for the exportation of fluid.
That section is also in the act at present; subsection 3 of my amendment is taken from the present act. The section in the present act states that without a licence no person shall construct or place in position any transmission line, and so on, and that implies that by granting a licence this parliament acquires legislative jurisdiction over the construction or placing in position of any such line. I suggest that parliament has no such legislative jurisdiction, except a declaration be made such as that proposed in the first subsection of this amendment.
The right hon. gentleman, in reading the opinion of Mr. Justice Duff, stated correctly that Mr. Justice Duff held that the construction of the line under section 92 (10) of the British North America Act applied only where the construction of a line was in contemplation. I submit that with regard to these transmission lines for the export of electrical energy, each and every one of them is in contemplation when this general act is passed, and that therefore the very fact that such lines are in contemplation, the very fact that the government assumes that it has the power of regulation with respect to those lines, shows that it is contemplated by this bill that such line or lines is or are about to be constructed. If the right hon. gentleman will assure us that, as long as he is Minister of Justice, in every private bill which is brought before the house a clause will be inserted to the effect that such line or lines as may be necessary to carry out the purposes of that private bill, for the exportation of electrical energy, shall be declared 
to be for the general advantage of Canada, the same purpose I have in mind undoubtedly will be served. But undoubtedly ministers of government change; others may hereafter sit in their seats. I trust that it will be a long time before there is any change concerning my right hon. friend, unless someone from this side of the house moves over there and holds the portfolio of the right hon. gentleman; but I think it would be advisable, even as a reminder, and it would have no ill effect, to insert a subsection such as the one I now propose in this amendment. If inserted in this bill, for greater caution, it will not serve to invalidate any other act on the statute books of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: TRANSFER TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY

subtopic: TRANSFER TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY

Sometimes i-t would be well, even if it were to throw a doubt upon the validity of prior legislation, that parliament, as in many cases similar, should make such legislation clear beyond all reasonable doubt, even though in some cases the change might be used as an argument by expert counsel. But I cannot conceive that, in dealing with a new matter such as this, in new legislation with regard to the export of power, and in placing such export within the jurisdiction of parliament, any reasonable precautions which we may now take would throw any doubt upon prior legislation.
Furthermore subsection 1 of section 8, as I have proposed it, will apply to all lines established for the exportation of power. It will not raise any doubt with regard to the application of the prior enactment, because the prior enactment will no longer be applicable even to lines already established. When once subsection 1 is enacted by parliament, it will apply to all lines in existence or in contemplation for the exportation of power. So that it is not a sufficient objection, I submit, to say that, simply because we are making section 8 clear now, it might be used by expert counsel as suggesting that prior legislation was invalid or defective. However, I do not intend to press the matter further. I have moved the amendment, and I was hoping the government would feel free to accept it.

Mr. Chairman, if I am in order I should like to make a few general observations with reference to the bill as a whole and to the objections that have been raised by hon. gentlemen opposite. I can well remember last year or 1935 when the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation was talking in reference to Beauharnois. He suggested that that undertaking be made a public utility and operated under government control. The right hon. leader of the opposition stated at the time- I hope I am quoting him correctly-that the parliament of Canada had no jurisdiction over the rivers and streams in the various provinces except those that were navigable waters, but it did have power to grant or to refuse licences for the export of power. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George has said that the frailties and faults of previous legislation should be avoided, but the question is whether the frailties and faults were in the amendment which he has withdrawn and not in this legislation.
Electric Power Export

I went to Toronto and had a conference with Premier Hepburn, but I did not go until I had spoken to the Prime Minister. I felt it was my duty to do that as a follower and supporter of his. He told me that he had absolutely no objection to my doing this. I pointed out to him that in Nova Scotia we had had considerable difficulty in connection with the hydro-electric development and with the Nova Scotia Tramways and Power Company in contradistinction to the Halifax Tramways Company. The latter corporation has a net capitalization of $2,000,000 as compared with the capitalization of $13,500,000 of the Nova Scotia Tramways and Power Company. Sufficient power has been developed at St. Margaret bay to run the trams, to light the city of Halifax and for domestic and industrial purposes at no cost to the city.
I felt that personal contact was the best means of ascertaining the position that one should take on a grave issue such as is involved in a private bill to enable Ontario to export its excess power to the United States. I may say that the premier of Ontario was open and above board, and he stated that the contract which he desired to make was a yearly one for a period not exceeding five years. He expected that by means of this contract some $14,000,000 could be made for the province, and he felt it to be his duty as premier to seek to export this surplus power. I felt then as I feel to-night, that if any industry, whether it be manufacturing or otherwise, produces more than the people of Canada can consume, there should be no law to prevent them from exporting their surplus to any country under the sun. I cannot understand why a fine distinction should be drawn between these two types of industry. My personal view is that Ontario should be permitted to export its surplus power to the United States or to any other country.
Last evening the Prime Minister tabled some correspondence in connection with something that is not yet in being. The only forgiving part of the documents tabled is the last letter written by Secretary of State, Mr. Cordell Hull, at the instance of President Roosevelt. That letter is dated March 17, a day on which everyone is convivial and more ready to forgive and forget. The government of the United States took that particular day on which to write to our representative at Washington, Sir Herbert Marler, the document which has been placed on the desk of every hon. member of this house. There is in that document something which seems to be foreign to the relationship that has existed between that great country and Canada. It speaks of the importation of

electrical energy from all foreign countries and Canada, a next door neighbour, part of the Anglo-Saxon race, and not foreign in the finer and the more noble sense of what we conceive to be the relationship which has existed in the past. Second, the president of the United States, through his Secretary of State, Mr. Cordell Hull, anticipated legislation being passed by this parliament, and plainly tells us, in cold, calm, black type, "You can pass any legislation you like, but you cannot put that power into my country," the United States, "unless you agree on the development of the deep waterway and making Fort William and Port Arthur the point of departure, passing the great city of Montreal and the city of Quebec as great shipping centres." Thank heaven, there is not a question that the maritimes are interested in that particular phase, although, speaking for myself and repeating the opinion of representative bodies, I believe the people of Nova Scotia are of the opinion that that development would be harmful to the Canadian ports.
I have a great respect for the president of the United States as well as for his Secretary of State, who is an outstanding statesman and a gentleman. Nevertheless, although they are 125 millions of people and we are only 11 millions, we have as much right in this parliament to express our opinion as to what we should do as they have to tell us what we should not do because if we do it we cannot "get by." It is like a sentry-go. The sentry stands at the gate and unless you have the pass word you cannot get in. Unless you have the password from the United States, electrical energy from Canada cannot go into that country, except under one condition, namely the development of the waterway, the development of the St. Lawrence to thirty feet, the deepening of the Welland canal- which has been done-and utilization by mutual understanding and by a distribution of the cost between the United States and Canada.
But let us not forget it is in contemplation -and I have this from those who know- that eventually through lake Erie a canal shall be built to the Hudson river and the shipping shall go down to the city of New York. Thereby our Canadian trade, which should go through Canadian ports, will be diverted through United States channels to United States ports, to the loss of our people who work on the waterfront, and our stevedores, and those whom they support, their wives and their children. Therefore I say that the legislation should stand or fall on its own merits, and without reference to these

Electric Power Export
absolutely dogmatic statements, spoken ex cathedra, that, "you shall not pass unless you do what we desire you to do, namely, carry out what we hope to get through congress, making a great waterway down the St. Lawrence river for the purpose of having ocean-going ships come up to Port Arthur and Fort William, to the neglect of the ports that are intervening on the great St. Lawrence river."
These, as I see them, are the facts. If I am wrong, hon. members can draw my attention either now or later to any mistake. I am always open to conviction, even to that which was said to me to-day that perhaps, instead of coming in at the door behind me, one of these days I might be coming in at the door opposite, and I said, "Well, if conditions changed I might be coming in at that door when I should have been coming in at this door." But that is just by the way I see no reason why I should change the door, and I see no great reason why the people of Canada should change the door either.
Under these conditions I would, if a private bill were introduced, vote to give Ontario the right to export its surplus power. I see in the press to-day a statement by the hon. member who resigned his seat in this house to become the leader of the Conservative party in Ontario, who "Rowe-d" himself from here to the capital of that province, there to sit as the leader of the Conservative party, with the design of later becoming premier. He rowed himself there; he rowed himself back, and he rowed himself into this house through the graciousness of the Prime Minister, the members of the government and others supporting the government, who gave him a seat in this house by acclamation. He goes back to Ontario and tells the people there that Mr. Hepburn does not represent anything, that he is a hydro-electric acrobat. If there is any greater acrobat than the hon. member, who is up there performing some acrobatic feats, and who is going to meet defeat, I should like to know what his recipe is, because some time, a hundred years from now, it might be that the Liberal party would need to use it, when we who are here have all gone and with us, our senses and knowledge of things on earth; we shall be in the-

The final point is this, that if we hope to keep the provinces of Canada together in their great confederacy, we must of necessity preserve local autonomy as well as the stronger legislative right of the parliament of Canada over matters of general concern. Matters that are set out in section 92 belong to the provinces, and the powers set out in section 91 are specifically within the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada; in the words of the leader of the opposition, "for greater certainty" it is in the British North America Act, in section 91, that all powers which are not within the purview of and set out in section 92 shall remain and be in the parliament of Canada. There we find the residuum of power in the federal government and in the government of the country-the government of to-day and of the future, which I believe will be the present government.
I desired to say what I have said only because I had an opportunity of discussing the matter with the premier of Ontario and I felt that, having done so if I sat in my seat and said nothing he would think I was like the young man of sixteen about to die. He ascended the scaffold; they put the black cap on his head and the noose around his neck, and the sheriff said to him, "Have you anything to say before we spring the trap?" He said, "Yes, I have. I am sixteen years old and about to die. So soon I am done for, I wonder what I was begun for." So let Mr. Rowe row himself back.

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, March 14, consideration of the motion of Mr. Dunning for committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Blackmore.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext:
When the house adjourned
on March 14, I was directing attention to certain matters in the absence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), and as I understand that some doubt has arisen as to the correctness of the observations which I made, I desire to point out just what the facts are, reading from the weekly report of the Bank of Canada.	.
On the 30th day of April, 1936, the weekly report was in form C of the statute creating the bank, and under the title, "Advances to provincial governments," there appears the sum of $2,000,000 total of such advances. The same continues in the issue of May 6, May 13. May 20, May 27; and on May 30 the amount is increased to $3,000,000 under item 4, subclause (b), provincial governments, $3,000,000, total, $3,000,000. That is on May 30. It continued to be $3,000,000 for the weeks ending Wednesday, June 3, June 10, June 17, with an advance of $300,000 on the last date also to chartered banks. It continued at $3,000,000, on June 24, June 30, July 8, July 15, July 22, July 29, July 31, August 5, August 12, August 19, August 26, August 31, being for the month. On September 2, being for the week ending on that Wednesday, it was still $3,000,000; on September 9, $3,000,000; on September 16, $3,000,000; on September 23, $3,000,000; on September 30, $3,000,000; on October 7, $3,000,000; on October 14, $3,000,000; on October 21, $3,000,000; and on October 28, $3,000,000. On October 31, being the monthly statement, the amount under item 4, provincial governments, is reduced to $1,000,000, and for the first time, for the week ending Wednesday, the 28t.h, it appears in an amended form. The reserves in sterling and United States dollars are combined into one amount, and the investments of dominion and provincial governments' short term securities are combined, and likewise with respect to dominion and provincial securities under (b). These are combined for the first time in the report of October 28, 1936. On October 31 the advances to provincial governments are reduced to $1,000,000. On November 4 the amount is still $1,000,000, and on November 10 and November 18 and November 25 it is still $1,000,000. In the monthly statement of the end of

November, 1936, that $1,000,000 disappears, since which time the form of C is, as I have indicated, amended by combining the reserves in sterling and United States dollars under one heading, and the investments in dominion and provincial short term and long term securities under one heading. The increase in dominion and provincial securities does not indicate whether or not it was brought about by the payment off of the $3,000,000 advances to provinces, but it does indicate an increase of that $1,000,000.
I desire to protest against the change of form in the Bank of Canada statement, the weekly statement and the monthly statement. We all know why the form was made as it was. It will be recalled that when the commission investigated the necessity for a central bank in Canada, one of our leading gentlemen of wide financial experience pointed out that there were grave dangers in permitting the purchase of sterling and United States exchange without some limitation being imposed upon the exercise of that right. Everyone in this country, be he banker or otherwise, looking at the form of statement which we appended to the Bank Act, could ascertain exactly at the end of each week how much was held in United States funds. He could know also the exact amount held in sterling. To-day the two are combined, and it is no longer possible for either banker or other individual to ascertain how the sum total of these two exchanges is made up.

I have a right to know that. Any man in this country has a right to know

it, because we have put our guarantee behind the deposits of the banks. The banks protested against leaving to the discretion of one or two men the acquisition of reserves either in sterling or in United States dollars for the purpose of creating the reserves which have the purpose indicated the other evening by the hon. .member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) Now we are told that these two must be combined. Well, I suppose, in due season we shall learn, because the government for some reason made the change.
We come now to the next point. The government still left the form as to. advances to the dominion government and provincial governments and chartered and savings banks as it was in schedule C of the original act. But when we come to deal with investments, the very difficulty which I pointed out has arisen, namely, including in investments dominion and provincial securities, short term and long term, a combination of the two without making it possible for any man to know what became of that $3,000,000 of advances to the provinces. Has not every citizen of this country, every person in every province of this dominion, the right to know why $3,000,000 is advanced to one province or two provinces,	and	other	provinces	are refusedadvances? How otherwise will he know it? Is that not the very purpose for which schedule C was provided, namely, that there should be a clear, distinct severance of the advances made under the item of investments for dominion government short term securities? They stood by themselves as item (a). Then we had (b), provincial government short term securities;	(c),	other	dominion	governmentsecurities;	(d),	other	provincial	governmentsecurities; (e), United Kingdom, other British dominions	or	United States securities of
maturities exceeding three months.
That has now been modified by order in council, and the form no longer enables me or any other member of this house or any member of the public to ascertain what sum has .been invested by the bank in the different classes of these securities, namely, short term dominion, short term provincial, long term dominion and long term provincial. That, I submit, is at variance with the very principles which underlie the maintenance of this bank. I want to make it clear that it is just such things as that which brought about the criticism of central banks. We are now
just starting with a central bank; it is desirable that we should not get into a position where criticism of a kind that has -been waged against some banks should be made against us. One of the important matters in connection with this legislation was that schedule C attached to the act made clear exactly what investments were made in the securities of provinces and the dominion, either short or long term.
I come now to another matter which should be considered. The other evening I pointed out that in dealing with the question of this bank there was a phase of it of which I wished to speak when the Minister of Finance was present. On July 5, 1935, we provided for the establishment of an exchange fund. Great criticism was waged against the government of the day because we provided that, when the gold in the hands of the banks or the dominion was realized, any profit should accrue to the dominion, after making provision for the foreign obligations of the banks at their branches in various parts of the world. The Minister of Finance finally arranged with the banks that forty per cent of their gold reserves should be kept by the banks for the purpose of providing for their foreign obligations; but sixty per cent of the gold held by the banks, as well as all the gold held by the Minister of Finance, passed into the hands of the Bank of Canada. Under the Exchange Fund Act, passed July 5, 1935, we provided that this gold should be converted at the then market price, and that the Minister of Finance should derive the benfit from the revaluation of that gold at the higher price. That, in fact, was done. In order that there may be no difficulty with respect to that, I direct attention to the language used by the governor of the bank at its annual meeting, so that we may have a clear appreciation of the fact that by legislation which we enacted in 1935, this country made a profit of $63,000,000 on its gold. At page 6 of the report of the governor of the bank to the first annual meeting, on February 25, 1936, we find these words:
Tlie largest item on the asset side of our balance sheet is gold, valued at $180,509,342. When we commenced operations we acquired gold to the value of $106,584,355, of which $69,455,439 came from the dominion government and $37,128,916 from the chartered banks. Settlement for this gold was effected on the basis of the statutory value of $20.67 an ounce. Subsequently, the Exchange Fund Act required us to value the gold at the current market price. The resultant profit of about $73,500,000 did not accrue to the Bank of Canada. Section 30 of the Bank of Canada Act had provided that any profits on gold transferred to the bank would pertain to the dominion government, but it gave the governor in council power to allow the chartered banks

to receive the profit on gold transferred by them, to the extent that sneh gold was deemed to have been held against liabilities elsewhere than in Canada. The governor in council determined that 40 per cent of the banks' gold had been so held, and as a result the chartered banks received $10,475,114. The balance of the profit, namely, $63,006,382, was credited to the exchange fund of the dominion government, and future profits or losses on gold held by us will be credited or debited to that account.
It should be noted that the valuation at which gold is entered on our balance sheet represents the amount which should be obtained in Canada if the gold were to be shipped to London or New York on the date of the statement. In other words, we apply the realizable value instead of an arbitrary one, and are not restricted to the price prevailing in any one particular market.
The point is that the report of the governor indicates that we made a profit of $63,000,000, and that future profits or losses on gold held by us will be credited or debited to that account. But last year I asked the government whether an order in council had been passed bringing section 6 of the Exchange Fund Act into force, and the answer was no. Section 6 of that act reads as follows:

It has a very direct bearing upon what was said by the hon. member for Rosthern and others in this house during the current session; for it meant that we had $63,000,000 available for the purposes of this country, any purpose that might be thought desirable in view of the fact that the

I desire now to direct attention to what I conceive to be a statement which may be very harmful, and I cannot think that the minister really meant it in the terms he used the other evening. I want to quote his exact words, in order that there may be no misunderstanding as to my correctly stating his position. I am now looking at page 1151 of Hansard. Dealing with the question of the 8350,000,000, the minister said:
An increase of say $350,000,000 in chartered bank holdings of Bank of Canada notes would increase their cash reserves from the present figure of about $250,000,000 to $600,000,000, and their cash ratio from about ten per cent to roughly twenty-one per cent.
The sponsor of the suggestion contends that no inflation is intended or would result by thus increasing bank cash, so long as the gold cover of the Bank of Canada did not fall below the twenty-five per cent minimum. This factor, however, is not a test of inflation. If the banks use their increased cash in the normal way, as a basis for the extension of roughly ten times as much in loans to the public, or for the acquisition of ten times as much in investments, bank deposits would expand by approximately an equal amount until the cash ratio was brought down again to approximately ten per cent. This would mean an increase in bank deposits from the present level of about $2,387,000,000 to something like $6,000,000,000, or more than 2-6 times the level of December 31, 1929. Am I merely old fashioned or orthodox when I say that this would mean a colossal measure of inflation?
I doubt if any observation more serious than that has been made by any responsible minister for a very long time. I remind the house that in 1932, when the empire agreements were being considered, the Liberal party voted to tie the dollar to the pound. They voted as a body to that effect. We resisted that; for to tie the dollar to the pound at that time would have done incalculable harm to this country, in view of what happened afterwards. We had on the one hand to pursue a course which would not raise exchange to any higher point than it had risen with the United States, where we had payments to make at that time in gold or its equivalent; and we had on the other hand to maintain our exchange position with Great Britain, Great Britain herself being in a most difficult position with respect to exchange. What did we do? We pursued the middle course, and we maintained so far as possible for our dollar a value that lay in between the pound on the one hand and the United States dollar on the other. Hon. members must know of the attention given to that matter by the Bank of Canada, which had to consider it on more than one occasion. I shall content myself with reading these words from page 13 of the first report of the Bank of Canada:
The Canadian dollar has exhibited a remarkable tendency, when not at parity with the pound or United States dollar, to take up an intermediate position. Obviously, in the long run, the purchasing power of our dollar must approximate that of the United States dollar and the pound sterling, or there would be a marked divergence in exchange rates. From the point of view of short term movements, it is probable that the large volume of United States and United Kingdom investments in Canada, and the existence of so many Canadian bonds payable in two or three currencies- a feature of our financial economy which is not found to an important degree in any other country-have had a tendency to restrict fluctuations in our exchange rate. A discount on the Canadian dollar in the United States encourages purchases of Canadian securities; a premium encourages selling; and the situation vis a vis the United Kingdom is the same.

The Minister of Finance must know exactly what the trend of the trade was when he left office. He knew that an adverse debt balance had been created in this country. He knew that we had this terrific responsibility with respect to interest charges on our obligations, private and public, as well as municipal in the markets of New York, and he knew also our position in Great Britain.
I have here a report issued by the statisticians of this country giving the story during all those years of what you might call the estimated British and foreign capital invested in capital investments abroad as at December 31, 1937, and preceding years, showing the slow progress that we made in being able to restore our credit position both in London and in New York.
